extraction.body: TODD BREASSEALE: Hey, good afternoon, everyone. Today we're going to discuss the Defense Intelligence Agency's release of its latest, unclassified, foundational report, “Challenges to Security in Space 2022.” This is the second edition of DIA’s series of reports designed to inform the public on key challenges and foreign military threats in space. DIA’s foundational reports foster informed dialogues between America's leaders, the national security community, warfighters, academia, allies and partners about key national security challenges facing the United States. We're joined today by DIA’s foremost experts in the space field, Dr. John Huth, DIA’s Defense Intelligence Officer for Space and Counterspace, and Mr. Kevin Ryder DIA Senior Defense Intelligence Analyst for Space and Counterspace. Gentlemen, I'll hand it over to you. DEFENSE INTELLIGENCE OFFICER DR. JOHN F. HUTH: Thank you for the opportunity to discuss DIA’s report that we're releasing today, “Challenges to Security in Space 2022.” This is an unclassified report and it's a follow-on to the first “Challenges to Security in Space” DIA released in 2019. Like its predecessor, this report examines the space and counterspace programs that pose or potentially pose a significant challenge to U.S. or partner interests by China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran. The second iteration addresses increases in the pace and scope of competitive space operations since early 2019, which you're about to hear have been dramatic. DIA produces reports that provide both broad overviews of country military capabilities known as the Military Power Series, and more narrowly focused functional threat reports such as “Challenges to Security in Space” and “Global Nuclear Landscapes.” These are designed to help the public achieve a deeper understanding of key challenges and threats to U.S. national security. This new edition of “Challenges to Security in Space” provides an updated unclassified overview of current threats to U.S. space-based capabilities. Particularly from China and Russia, but also to a lesser extent, those emerging from North Korea and Iran. This edition examines the expansion of space operations and details Earth-focused space services, as well as growing efforts to explore the moon and beyond. And it also includes an expanded assessment of impacts of space debris. Space-based capabilities impact many day-to-day aspects of the American way of life. They enable functions that affect our homes, transportation, electric power grids, banking and communications. From watching television, to predicting weather patterns to avoiding traffic on our daily commutes, satellites enable many real-time conveniences that have become integral to our daily lives. On the national security front, space-based capabilities afford the United States and our allies with crucial ability to project combat power to areas of conflict and instability. They enable our armed forces to collect vital intelligence on foreign threats, navigate and maneuver rapidly, and communicate with one another to support global military and humanitarian crises. Meanwhile, Russia and China, our primary strategic competitors, are taking steps to undercut the United States and our allies in the space domain. Both nations view space as a requirement for winning modern wars, especially against Western nations, and look to prove themselves as world leaders. Since early 2019, competitor space operations have increased in pace and scope across nearly all major categories — communications, remote sensing, navigation, and science and technology demonstration. SENIOR DEFENSE ANALYST KEVIN RYDER: And China and Russia value superiority in space. And as a result, they'll seek ways to strengthen their space and counter-space programs and determine better ways to integrate them within their respective militaries. Both nations seek to broaden their space exploration initiatives together and individually with plans to explore the moon and Mars during the next 30 years. And if successful, these efforts will likely lead to attempts by Beijing and Moscow to exploit the moon's natural resources. Beijing and Moscow have integrated space-based capabilities into their individual, national and warfighting strategies with the intent of denying the United States a space-enabled advantage. Evidence of both nations’ intent to undercut the United States and allied leadership in the space domain can be seen in the growth of combined in-orbit assets of China and Russia, which grew approximately 70% in just two years. This recent and continuing expansion follows a more than 200% increase between 2015 and 2018. China has launched a robotic lander and rover to the far side of the moon, and an orbiter lander and rover in one mission to Mars. It has also launched multiple missiles, capable of destroying satellites, and deployed mobile jammers to deny satellite communications and GPS. Moscow on the other hand, has developed a suite of counter-space weapons capabilities, including electronic warfare, to deny, degrade, and disrupt communications, and to not - to deny the use of space-based imagery. Russia is also developing a mobile missile that is able to destroy satellites and crewed space vehicles. Now as the number of spacefaring nations grow, and counter-space capabilities become more integrated into military operations, the U.S. Space Posture will be increasingly challenged and orbit assets will face new risk. A secure, stable, and accessible space domain is crucial as challenges to the United States and our allies’ space capabilities continue to increase. “Challenges to Security in Space — 2022” offs the insights from top intelligence experts on current threats to the United States Space Posture posed by our strategic competitors, and key space issues through 2030 and beyond. Thank you for your time, we will now take questions. MR. BREASSEALE: So, if you have a question for these gentlemen, please just raise your hand and I'll call on you. And you can please state your name and outlet for which you're reporting. I saw your hand first. Yes, ma'am. Q: Hi, Tara Copp with Defense One. I was wondering if you could both talk about the extent to which China has been watching Russia's invasion of Ukraine and how it's shaping what counter-space capabilities it's pursuing? And what sort of - is it gathering lessons learned? Will it make it more difficult in future conflicts based on what we've seen happen over Ukraine? DR. HUTH: So, as far as the scope of the document really doesn't cover that, that's fairly new, and I’ll say, evolving information. So, really don't have a whole lot to – to add on that right now. MR. RYDER: So, I will say that, from a DIA perspective, what we do is we provide information on the threats and the challenges that are posed by our adversaries. And we provide that to our policymakers and our warfighting planners to make those determinations on the type of systems and mitigation strategies that are needed. DR. HUTH: And certainly, the acquisition community, the NRO [National Reconnaissance Office], SDA – Space Development Agency, et cetera. But as Kevin said, that's really for us to inform them. It's for them to figure out, based on that threat information, what they want to do. MR. BREASSEALE: Let’s take a caller, Theresa Hitchens, from Breaking Defense. MR. BREASSEALE: I want to go to the phones real quickly. Bill Gertz, Washington Times. Q: Yes. Hi. I want to follow up on Tony's question on the fractional orbital launch. Can you say whether this is a nuclear system, or it's a conventional system? And it is reported in the report as part of space weapons that are used to hit targets on the earth, on the sea and in the air. Can you elaborate a little bit more on that? MR. RYDER: Could you repeat the question? I'm sorry. And I know, Ukraine happened after this is published, but to the extent that that is occurring on the current battlefield, what sort of guidance are you providing, or helping shape future U.S. defenses for future potential conflict? DR. HUTH: So again, I'd say the report, and the information from an intelligence perspective stands as it is. So those types of things are what we provide to our customers, for them to consider as they are acquiring new capabilities with the understanding that both China and Russia are expanding their kit, if you will, in counter-space capabilities. And those are all factored into design of U.S. systems. MR. BREASSEALE: Let's go to the phones again. Poonam Sharma from Global Straits. MR. RYDER: So, from my perspective, all of the capabilities are equal in nature. It depends on how and why and when the adversary would tend to use them or choose to use them. DR. HUTH: And if I could just reemphasize my last point and pile on what Kevin said. So, it's not just a capability, it's the fact that they have a space force or each have space forces, China and Russia. And their intent is to make space part of that combined arms effort in any conflict. Q: Can I follow up on that a little bit, on John's question? Which capability are they the most advanced in, that's the most alarming to you? Q: Thank you so much. Just a couple of short questions. Does DIA also produce a classified version of this report or just the unclassified? And the second part of the question, in your discussion on China's capabilities, do you consider all Chinese space capabilities military? Or do you make a distinction between civilian space and military space? Thank you. MR. RYDER: So, for your first question, while DIA does publish a number of classified documents, “Challenges to Security in Space” is only produced in an unclassified format. DR. HUTH: I think with regard to your second question, Kevin, and I think I, had already both talked about what the Chinese refer to as civil-military fusion. So sometimes, things can look very distinct as to whether they lay on one side or another, at least for the time being. And that can change because of that, and there's a lot of gray area in there. They - they don't conduct business the way - certainly the way the U.S. or other Western countries do. Q: Hi, I'm Luis Martinez with ABC News. I have two questions. One, how does - in terms of the counter-space activities we're seeing from Russia and China, how does this report compare with what the conclusions from the 2019 report? You know, broad strokes, what's the main difference between those two? MR. RYDER: Well, as you said, 2022 builds on our 2019 report. It expands a little bit more on some of the future developments. It also takes a harder look at space debris and the causes - the potential impact of that in space. And it also looks at development to get out - exploration out beyond the moon. DR. HUTH: And I think we go a little bit deeper on space domain awareness and command and control as well in the new report.

passages: If Lockdown Mode sounds aggressive, it's because that's exactly what it was designed for.
Back in 2023, an exploit known as "Blastpass" used iMessage to install the Pegasus spyware on Apple devices .
However, researchers found that devices in Lockdown Mode were completely immune to the spyware.
Apple offers a 100 percent bonus on top of the regular reward through its Security Bounty program to anyone who finds a way to bypass the feature, which shows how much the company trusts it.
By restricting your iPhone to avoid potential attack vectors, you're given maximum security in exchange for reduced functionality and convenience.
The iPhone's Lockdown Mode has been around since 2022 , but you might not have heard about it, let alone used it.
Apple itself calls the tool an "extreme" layer of security for the few people who may be targeted by commercial spyware such as NSO's Pegasus .
Journalists, activists and politicians are among the potential targets of such spyware.
Anyone with an iPhone running iOS 16 or newer can try out Lockdown Mode.
It's also available on iPadOS 16 and later, watchOS 10 and newer, and macOS 13 Ventura and later.
To turn it on, open Settings and go to Privacy & Security .
Scroll down until you find Lockdown Mode , then tap Turn On & Restart and confirm with your passcode.
It's simple as that, and you'll find the option to disable it in the same place.
However, many of those features are ones you likely use every day.
In Messages, most kinds of attachments are blocked.
Even link previews stop working, since they can serve as a backdoor for spyware.
Lockdown Mode also restricts how JavaScript works in browsers, which may cause some websites to load slowly or not work at all.
FaceTime calls are also blocked; only people you've called recently can reach you.
For most people, there's no need to use Lockdown Mode.
Apple devices already have many security and privacy features built in.
Spyware like Pegasus usually targets public figures and is often deployed by governments that want to spy on opponents or protesters.
Chances are that the inconveniences it creates are not worth the extreme level of protection that few people need.
For instance, wired connections are disabled when the device is locked — meaning it cannot communicate with a computer or accessory without your passcode.

For wireless connectivity, your iPhone will no longer automatically connect to unsecured networks, and support for 2G and 3G networks is completely disabled (though these networks were discontinued in the US years ago).
If you have an Apple Watch, phone call notifications from your iPhone won't show up on it.

extraction.body: Lockdown Mode makes your iPhone much more secure against spyware, but most people don't need to use it. The iPhone's Lockdown Mode has been around since 2022 , but you might not have heard about it, let alone used it. It's one of those features that's well-hidden in the Settings app, plus it's not really meant for the average person. Apple itself calls the tool an "extreme" layer of security for the few people who may be targeted by commercial spyware such as NSO's Pegasus . Journalists, activists and politicians are among the potential targets of such spyware. Anyone with an iPhone running iOS 16 or newer can try out Lockdown Mode. It's also available on iPadOS 16 and later, watchOS 10 and newer, and macOS 13 Ventura and later. To turn it on, open Settings and go to Privacy & Security . Scroll down until you find Lockdown Mode , then tap Turn On & Restart and confirm with your passcode. It's simple as that, and you'll find the option to disable it in the same place. What makes Lockdown Mode strong is how it blocks many of the iPhone's features when enabled. However, many of those features are ones you likely use every day. In Messages, most kinds of attachments are blocked. Even link previews stop working, since they can serve as a backdoor for spyware. Lockdown Mode also restricts how JavaScript works in browsers, which may cause some websites to load slowly or not work at all. FaceTime calls are also blocked; only people you've called recently can reach you. Your iPhone's connectivity is also limited when Lockdown Mode is on. For instance, wired connections are disabled when the device is locked — meaning it cannot communicate with a computer or accessory without your passcode. For wireless connectivity, your iPhone will no longer automatically connect to unsecured networks, and support for 2G and 3G networks is completely disabled (though these networks were discontinued in the US years ago). You also can't install configuration profiles, which isn't ideal if your school or employer requires one. If you have an Apple Watch, phone call notifications from your iPhone won't show up on it. You'll see reduced functionality across other Apple services too: Home invitations and Game Center are not available, and photo sharing is restricted. The feature offers some flexibility: you can exclude certain contacts from messaging restrictions so your family can still send you videos or documents. passages: I put my Pixel into lockdown mode every night before bed, and again every time I left the house for a week.l The first couple of days took a little cognitive effort to remember to do it, but typing the PIN in to unlock was like revisiting an old friend.
I was fully ok with it after day three; it just felt like the biometrics weren't working and typing in the 6-digit number was seamless (fine, i forgot a couple of times, sheesh).
The only friction was the Lock Screen Notification suppression, to be honest.
I've come to rely on those to let me know what's happening on my phone without having to open it up.
Still, it's a much stronger security feature , especially if I'm at a protest (I live in Portland, so that's fairly often).
It's something I wish my iPhone had going for it.
My OnePlus Open doesn't have a lockdown mode, either.
Lockdown mode asks very little of me: a simple button press, tap, then unlock with a PIN.
The protection it offers against compelled biometric access is real and unfortunately fairly relevant lately here in the U.S. at least.
If you have a Pixel and travel or hit a protest or two, this is worth making a habit.
The fastest way to enable lockdown mode on a Google Pixel is by pressing the Volume up and Power buttons .
You'll see a slider to Power off your iPhone, one to bring up your Medical ID, and one to activate an SOS Emergency Call.
If you hit Cancel, your iPhone will require your pass code before going back to FaceID mode.
Before you come at me, though, and say "this is the same thing as Pixel," I'll respectfully disagree.
There's nothing clear about the iOS solution, even if functionally it does similar.
Lockdown on Pixel actually locks your phone immediately, no Cancel button needed.
Lockdown mode resets automatically on the next unlock.
The Google Pixel 10a is a budget-oriented smartphone with a flat back and long battery life.
It's powered by the same Tensor G4 chip as its predecessor, and many key specs are identical to the Pixel 9a.
However, you do get a brighter screen, better modem, new software features, and Android 16 with seven years of software support.

extraction.body: Rob LeFebvre is an editor and writer focusing on consumer and enterprise technologies for a broad range of outlets. He’s been writing online for more than 15 years; before that he was a special educator for kids with severe disabilities. Rob has been an Editorial Director at Lifewire, a news writer at Engadget, and a senior contributor at Cult of Mac. He's written about PCs, Macs, mobile phones, and games, created newsrooms from the ground up, and has extensive experience reviewing hardware, software, and games across his career. Unlocking your phone with your face or fingerprint is easy, useful, and fast, but it also makes it easier for others to access your phone. All they need to do is swipe your fingerprint real fast, or aim the phone at your face, and they're in. Passcodes are much harder to force you to enter, and courts are much more willing to protect them under the Fifth Amendment. Google's stock Android phone, the Pixel, includes a feature called lockdown mode, and it's a fantastic way to quickly and temporarily require a pass code to unlock it. I used it for a week to see how much of a hassle it is, and frankly, it's become my favorite way to safeguard my info when I'm out and about. It's something I wish my iPhone had going for it. The fastest way to enable lockdown mode on a Google Pixel is by pressing the Volume up and Power buttons . Holding the power button down just pulls up Gemini, so be sure to use both buttons. The feature is available by default, so you don't have to go searching through the Settings app to enable it. It disables all fingerprint and face unlock systems and forces you to use your pass code to unlock the phone. It also disables Extend Unlock/Smart Lock so that any of your trusted locations or Bluetooth devices won't allow access to your phone, and it hides all lock screen notifications so content can't be read without unlocking. Lockdown mode resets automatically on the next unlock. Biometrics and lock screens all return to normal until you enable lockdown mode again. When you do lock it down, nothing is affected inside the phone — all your apps, data, Google Wallet, etc. will continue to work as usual. None of the following is legal advice. If you need that, you'll need to find a lawyer who specializes in this area. That said, courts have generally held that a PIN is knowledge from the mind, called testimonial, and is therefore protected under the FIfth Amendment (which protects against self-incrimination). It's not ironclad, though, as the 9th Circuit ruled that compelled fingerprint unlock is non-testimonial , while the D.C. CIrcuit ruled the opposite in 2025. Bottom line, you're likely safer when using a PIN instead of a biometric unlock like fingerprints or face recognition. If you're crossing a border, CBP (Customs and Border Protection) has broad authority to search devices at the border without a warrant . Protest arrests are another time and place where your phone can be routinely searched and biometrics can be applied while you are physically restrained. You'll definitely want to set your phone to lockdown at least if you attend a protest . The Google Pixel 10a is a budget-oriented smartphone with a flat back and long battery life. It's powered by the same Tensor G4 chip as its predecessor, and many key specs are identical to the Pixel 9a. However, you do get a brighter screen, better modem, new software features, and Android 16 with seven years of software support. I rock an iPhone 15 Pro Max as my daily handset, and while I know you can turn off FaceID on iOS, that's a fully nuclear option that, while useful, doesn't have the same nuance as Pixel's solution. My OnePlus Open doesn't have a lockdown mode, either. iOS has an Emergency SOS feature that you can activate by pressing the power button five times in a row. You'll see a slider to Power off your iPhone, one to bring up your Medical ID, and one to activate an SOS Emergency Call. If you hit Cancel, your iPhone will require your pass code before going back to FaceID mode. Before you come at me, though, and say "this is the same thing as Pixel," I'll respectfully disagree. There's nothing clear about the iOS solution, even if functionally it does similar. Lockdown on Pixel actually locks your phone immediately, no Cancel button needed. We all used to use PIN codes to get into our phones. Heck, when FaceID doesn't work, thanks to sunglasses or weird lighting, you've got to put it in, anyway. I put my Pixel into lockdown mode every night before bed, and again every time I left the house for a week.l The first couple of days took a little cognitive effort to remember to do it, but typing the PIN in to unlock was like revisiting an old friend. I was fully ok with it after day three; it just felt like the biometrics weren't working and typing in the 6-digit number was seamless (fine, i forgot a couple of times, sheesh). The only friction was the Lock Screen Notification suppression, to be honest. I've come to rely on those to let me know what's happening on my phone without having to open it up. Still, it's a much stronger security feature , especially if I'm at a protest (I live in Portland, so that's fairly often). Doing it this way, instead of just turning off biometrics, made it feel more like a ritual, one more thing to do before events like protests or border crossings. It also lets you keep the biometrics on most of the time, because hopefully most of us aren't under constant threat of hving our phones unlocked for evidence. For me, the answer here is yes. Lockdown mode asks very little of me: a simple button press, tap, then unlock with a PIN. It's easy to do and a little simpler than the five button press on my iPhone (which doesn't lead to a clear press anyway). The protection it offers against compelled biometric access is real and unfortunately fairly relevant lately here in the U.S. at least. The iPhone's Lockdown Mode has been around since 2022 , but you might not have heard about it, let alone used it. It's one of those features that's well-hidden in the Settings app, plus it's not really meant for the average person. Scroll down until you find Lockdown Mode , then tap Turn On & Restart and confirm with your passcode. It's simple as that, and you'll find the option to disable it in the same place. What makes Lockdown Mode strong is how it blocks many of the iPhone's features when enabled. However, many of those features are ones you likely use every day. In Messages, most kinds of attachments are blocked. Even link previews stop working, since they can serve as a backdoor for spyware. Lockdown Mode also restricts how JavaScript works in browsers, which may cause some websites to load slowly or not work at all. For instance, wired connections are disabled when the device is locked — meaning it cannot communicate with a computer or accessory without your passcode. You also can't install configuration profiles, which isn't ideal if your school or employer requires one. If you have an Apple Watch, phone call notifications from your iPhone won't show up on it. You'll see reduced functionality across other Apple services too: Home invitations and Game Center are not available, and photo sharing is restricted. Apple itself calls the tool an "extreme" layer of security for the few people who may be targeted by commercial spyware such as NSO's Pegasus . Journalists, activists and politicians are among the potential targets of such spyware.

Anyone with an iPhone running iOS 16 or newer can try out Lockdown Mode. It's also available on iPadOS 16 and later, watchOS 10 and newer, and macOS 13 Ventura and later. To turn it on, open Settings and go to Privacy & Security . Scroll down until you find Lockdown Mode , then tap Turn On & Restart and confirm with your passcode. It's simple as that, and you'll find the option to disable it in the same place.

What makes Lockdown Mode strong is how it blocks many of the iPhone's features when enabled. However, many of those features are ones you likely use every day. In Messages, most kinds of attachments are blocked. Even link previews stop working, since they can serve as a backdoor for spyware. Lockdown Mode also restricts how JavaScript works in browsers, which may cause some websites to load slowly or not work at all. FaceTime calls are also blocked; only people you've called recently can reach you.

Your iPhone's connectivity is also limited when Lockdown Mode is on. For instance, wired connections are disabled when the device is locked — meaning it cannot communicate with a computer or accessory without your passcode. For wireless connectivity, your iPhone will no longer automatically connect to unsecured networks, and support for 2G and 3G networks is completely disabled (though these networks were discontinued in the US years ago).

You also can't install configuration profiles, which isn't ideal if your school or employer requires one. If you have an Apple Watch, phone call notifications from your iPhone won't show up on it. You'll see reduced functionality across other Apple services too: Home invitations and Game Center are not available, and photo sharing is restricted.

If Lockdown Mode sounds aggressive, it's because that's exactly what it was designed for. Back in 2023, an exploit known as "Blastpass" used iMessage to install the Pegasus spyware on Apple devices . However, researchers found that devices in Lockdown Mode were completely immune to the spyware. Apple offers a 100 percent bonus on top of the regular reward through its Security Bounty program to anyone who finds a way to bypass the feature, which shows how much the company trusts it. By restricting your iPhone to avoid potential attack vectors, you're given maximum security in exchange for reduced functionality and convenience.

The feature offers some flexibility: you can exclude certain contacts from messaging restrictions so your family can still send you videos or documents. You also have the option to exclude certain websites and apps from the feature. However, loosening these restrictions makes your device a little more vulnerable to attacks. If you think you're a target, it's best to keep all the default protections turned on.

For most people, there's no need to use Lockdown Mode. Apple devices already have many security and privacy features built in. Spyware like Pegasus usually targets public figures and is often deployed by governments that want to spy on opponents or protesters. If that's the case for you, it's definitely worth turning on Lockdown Mode — Apple may even send you a notification if it believes you've been targeted by spyware . If you're curious, try using Lockdown Mode for a few days to see what it's like. Chances are that the inconveniences it creates are not worth the extreme level of protection that few people need.

sources.title: I used Pixel's lockdown mode for a week, and it solves a problem Apple hasn't - MakeUseOf
passages: I put my Pixel into lockdown mode every night before bed, and again every time I left the house for a week.l The first couple of days took a little cognitive effort to remember to do it, but typing the PIN in to unlock was like revisiting an old friend.
I was fully ok with it after day three; it just felt like the biometrics weren't working and typing in the 6-digit number was seamless (fine, i forgot a couple of times, sheesh).
The only friction was the Lock Screen Notification suppression, to be honest.
I've come to rely on those to let me know what's happening on my phone without having to open it up.
Still, it's a much stronger security feature , especially if I'm at a protest (I live in Portland, so that's fairly often).
It's something I wish my iPhone had going for it.
My OnePlus Open doesn't have a lockdown mode, either.
Lockdown mode asks very little of me: a simple button press, tap, then unlock with a PIN.
The protection it offers against compelled biometric access is real and unfortunately fairly relevant lately here in the U.S. at least.
If you have a Pixel and travel or hit a protest or two, this is worth making a habit.
The fastest way to enable lockdown mode on a Google Pixel is by pressing the Volume up and Power buttons .
You'll see a slider to Power off your iPhone, one to bring up your Medical ID, and one to activate an SOS Emergency Call.
If you hit Cancel, your iPhone will require your pass code before going back to FaceID mode.
Before you come at me, though, and say "this is the same thing as Pixel," I'll respectfully disagree.
There's nothing clear about the iOS solution, even if functionally it does similar.
Lockdown on Pixel actually locks your phone immediately, no Cancel button needed.
Lockdown mode resets automatically on the next unlock.
The Google Pixel 10a is a budget-oriented smartphone with a flat back and long battery life.
It's powered by the same Tensor G4 chip as its predecessor, and many key specs are identical to the Pixel 9a.
However, you do get a brighter screen, better modem, new software features, and Android 16 with seven years of software support.
The best of MakeUseOf, directly in your inbox.
Don't forget about repair mode too - locks your internal files down until you unlock it with a passcode - added security

You'll see a slider to Power off your iPhone, one to bring up your Medical ID, and one to activate an SOS Emergency Call.
If you hit Cancel, your iPhone will require your pass code before going back to FaceID mode.
Before you come at me, though, and say "this is the same thing as Pixel," I'll respectfully disagree.
There's nothing clear about the iOS solution, even if functionally it does similar.
Lockdown on Pixel actually locks your phone immediately, no Cancel button needed.
Lockdown mode resets automatically on the next unlock.
The Google Pixel 10a is a budget-oriented smartphone with a flat back and long battery life.
It's powered by the same Tensor G4 chip as its predecessor, and many key specs are identical to the Pixel 9a.
However, you do get a brighter screen, better modem, new software features, and Android 16 with seven years of software support.
Don't forget about repair mode too - locks your internal files down until you unlock it with a passcode - added security

extraction.body: Starting this winter, a new weather enhancement pilot program is planning to test whether a new technology can increase snowpack and rainfall across just shy of 200,000 acres of Northwest Colorado’s Flat Tops — an area that includes the Yampa River headwaters. The one-year pilot, which is funded by a $100,000 grant from the Colorado Water Conservation Board to the Upper Yampa Water Conservancy District, plans to test a ground-based, solar-powered technology from Rain Enhancement Technologies . It would be the state of Colorado’s ninth permitted weather modification project, according to a news release from Rain Enhancement Technologies. It would join permitted cloud-seeding projects at ski areas like Vail Mountain, Beaver Creek Resort, Breckenridge Ski Resort, Keystone Resort and Winter Park Resort, in the San Juan Mountains as well as a project conducted by Rain Enhancement Technologies in Weld County, among others. The partners have been moving through the leasing and permitting requirements to begin installation — and, hopefully, storm enhancement — in November. Standing at Yamcolo Reservoir just below the Yampa River’s headwaters in August, Andy Rossi, the Upper Yampa district’s general manager, described the technology as “brand new and experimental.” “As we move into drier and drier times, folks like us, we’ve got to keep trying new things,” Rossi said. “We don’t know if it works yet, but we’re willing to give it a shot and do the research behind it and see if it’s worth continuing later out for a couple of decades.” Collecting snowmelt from its headwaters in the Flat Tops, the Yampa River flows east to Stagecoach Reservoir, where it makes a U-turn and meanders west into Dinosaur National Monument and merges with the Green River, and eventually, the Colorado River. The White River also has its headwaters in the Flat Tops and empties into the Green River farther west in Utah. Combined and depending on the year, Rossi said these two rivers comprise 10-15% of the flow at Lee Ferry, just downstream of Lake Powell. “Without snow, this whole system doesn’t really work,” Rossi said, adding that the goal of the pilot is to “hopefully create a little bit more bang for a buck out of each storm track that comes through, both rain and snow.” The need for this kind of innovation was illustrated after this year saw Colorado’s worst snowpack on record , abnormally hot temperatures and historically low streamflows spiral the state — particularly its northwest corner — into deeper drought . “We have been able to track changes in snowpack, in temperatures and in climate variability in our basin, and indeed, what it has shown us over the past decade or so is that the area of the Flat Tops, and at the very highest end of the headwaters of the Yampa, is experiencing a higher degree of warming and a higher degree of snowpack modification because of warming conditions,” Rossi said in an October interview. “For us to target an area that needs the most help, that’s it.” Compared to “typical” cloud-seeding technology, which involves injecting tiny particles — most commonly silver iodide crystals — into clouds to enhance their precipitation potential, this ground-based technology uses ionization to target a similar effect. Rain Enhancement Technologies calls it the Weather Enhancement Technology Array. In an October interview, Rossi said the installation will be about 30 feet wide and 20 feet long and resembles a ranch gate, with a large frame and electrified coil. It relies entirely on solar power. According to the statement of work for the pilot, “each station releases electrically charged negative ions into naturally occurring wind flow feeding the cloud with the ‘fuel’ needed to cultivate precipitation.” These charges enter the cloud mass and enhance condensation, causing cloud droplets to “progressively grow” until they are large and heavy enough to fall as precipitation, it adds. Meteorologists and technicians with Rain Enhancement Technology will then track storms remotely, firing up the apparatus “when they see a storm track that is: one, headed in the right direction … and two, it has the right predicted moisture content there,” Rossi said. A test of the technology outside of Moab, Utah, reportedly led the snow-water equivalent to increase by over 20%. Andrew Rickert, Colorado’s weather modification program manager, said in April that more traditional cloud-seeding systems can increase a storm’s snowfall by roughly 8-12% when generators are turned on. The Upper Yampa installation will be located at Colorado Parks and Wildlife’s State Wildlife Area near Lake Avery, with the intent of increasing precipitation in a 200,000-acre area of the Flat Tops and into the basin. The ability to be “very specific about the area we were trying to influence” was one of the things that appealed to Rossi about the technology when he was approached midsummer by the Colorado Water Conservation Board and Colorado River District about potentially piloting it. “We, at the Upper Yampa District, are really trying to enhance the water supply for our reservoirs, and for the headwaters, snowpack, water supply that drives the whole upper end of the system,” he added. “There’s water scarcity that has been going on for generations up there, and so it really was the best place for us to try to deploy a new technology … and try to push the envelope a little bit in response to droughts.” In a news release, Scott Morris, vice president of engineering at Rain Enhancement Technologies, said that “beyond the reservoirs downstream, this site gives us a chance to benefit the land right around it.” “We’ll be operating to provide some enhancement to Lake Avery, which is right near the site, and we expect more rainfall and snowpack over the surrounding wilderness areas, which should benefit the forests and the wildlife there,” Morris said. Rossi added that the site was also carefully selected so as not to increase moisture and precipitation on the burn scars from the Elk and Lee fires, which burned outside of Meeker in 2025. “That landscape needs some time to heal, and we wanted to be sure we weren’t creating an unintended consequence there that would be negative to that landscape,” he said. The state has other guidelines to ensure weather modification technologies do not have negative impacts. Rossi said this includes shutting down the project if snowpack gets too high or robust as well as shutting down for “very volatile storm tracks” with the potential for high-intensity rainfall and flash flooding. “There is a component of safety that is offering a nice check valve on how much we try to influence the moisture that could fall as precipitation,” he said. The pilot program will last an entire year, meaning that the pilot will aim to track the “efficacy of the technology” and whether there is a “quantifiable positive impact” to both rain and snow precipitation,” Rossi said. Testing this new technology is just one way the water conservancy district is looking to build resilienc y in the face of drought. “It really is an excellent opportunity for us to try one of the new technologies or methods that’s out there in response to drought,” Rossi said. “This is something that I think we’re gonna need to keep searching for solutions to, and if we can feel like we’ve tried everything that is reasonable, I think we’re gonna feel a little bit better about trying to manage the water resources for the district and for the water users within the district.” As a Summit Daily News reader, you make our work possible. The full project is expected to cost about $165,000. All donations made in 2023 will go directly toward this project. Every contribution, no matter the size, will make a difference.

Collecting snowmelt from its headwaters in the Flat Tops, the Yampa River flows east to Stagecoach Reservoir, where it makes a U-turn and meanders west into Dinosaur National Monument and merges with the Green River, and eventually, the Colorado River. The White River also has its headwaters in the Flat Tops and empties into the Green River farther west in Utah. Combined and depending on the year, Rossi said these two rivers comprise 10-15% of the flow at Lee Ferry, just downstream of Lake Powell.

“Without snow, this whole system doesn’t really work,” Rossi said, adding that the goal of the pilot is to “hopefully create a little bit more bang for a buck out of each storm track that comes through, both rain and snow.”

The need for this kind of innovation was illustrated after this year saw Colorado’s worst snowpack on record , abnormally hot temperatures and historically low streamflows spiral the state — particularly its northwest corner — into deeper drought .

“We have been able to track changes in snowpack, in temperatures and in climate variability in our basin, and indeed, what it has shown us over the past decade or so is that the area of the Flat Tops, and at the very highest end of the headwaters of the Yampa, is experiencing a higher degree of warming and a higher degree of snowpack modification because of warming conditions,” Rossi said in an October interview. “For us to target an area that needs the most help, that’s it.”

Compared to “typical” cloud-seeding technology, which involves injecting tiny particles — most commonly silver iodide crystals — into clouds to enhance their precipitation potential, this ground-based technology uses ionization to target a similar effect. Rain Enhancement Technologies calls it the Weather Enhancement Technology Array.

In an October interview, Rossi said the installation will be about 30 feet wide and 20 feet long and resembles a ranch gate, with a large frame and electrified coil. It relies entirely on solar power.

According to the statement of work for the pilot, “each station releases electrically charged negative ions into naturally occurring wind flow feeding the cloud with the ‘fuel’ needed to cultivate precipitation.”
These charges enter the cloud mass and enhance condensation, causing cloud droplets to “progressively grow” until they are large and heavy enough to fall as precipitation, it adds.

Meteorologists and technicians with Rain Enhancement Technology will then track storms remotely, firing up the apparatus “when they see a storm track that is: one, headed in the right direction … and two, it has the right predicted moisture content there,” Rossi said.

A test of the technology outside of Moab, Utah, reportedly led the snow-water equivalent to increase by over 20%. Andrew Rickert, Colorado’s weather modification program manager, said in April that more traditional cloud-seeding systems can increase a storm’s snowfall by roughly 8-12% when generators are turned on.

The Upper Yampa installation will be located at Colorado Parks and Wildlife’s State Wildlife Area near Lake Avery, with the intent of increasing precipitation in a 200,000-acre area of the Flat Tops and into the basin.

The ability to be “very specific about the area we were trying to influence” was one of the things that appealed to Rossi about the technology when he was approached midsummer by the Colorado Water Conservation Board and Colorado River District about potentially piloting it.

“We, at the Upper Yampa District, are really trying to enhance the water supply for our reservoirs, and for the headwaters, snowpack, water supply that drives the whole upper end of the system,” he added. “There’s water scarcity that has been going on for generations up there, and so it really was the best place for us to try to deploy a new technology … and try to push the envelope a little bit in response to droughts.”

In a news release, Scott Morris, vice president of engineering at Rain Enhancement Technologies, said that “beyond the reservoirs downstream, this site gives us a chance to benefit the land right around it.”

“We’ll be operating to provide some enhancement to Lake Avery, which is right near the site, and we expect more rainfall and snowpack over the surrounding wilderness areas, which should benefit the forests and the wildlife there,” Morris said.
Rossi added that the site was also carefully selected so as not to increase moisture and precipitation on the burn scars from the Elk and Lee fires, which burned outside of Meeker in 2025.
“That landscape needs some time to heal, and we wanted to be sure we weren’t creating an unintended consequence there that would be negative to that landscape,” he said.

The state has other guidelines to ensure weather modification technologies do not have negative impacts. Rossi said this includes shutting down the project if snowpack gets too high or robust as well as shutting down for “very volatile storm tracks” with the potential for high-intensity rainfall and flash flooding.
“There is a component of safety that is offering a nice check valve on how much we try to influence the moisture that could fall as precipitation,” he said.

The pilot program will last an entire year, meaning that the pilot will aim to track the “efficacy of the technology” and whether there is a “quantifiable positive impact” to both rain and snow precipitation,” Rossi said.
Testing this new technology is just one way the water conservancy district is looking to build resilienc y in the face of drought.

“It really is an excellent opportunity for us to try one of the new technologies or methods that’s out there in response to drought,” Rossi said. “This is something that I think we’re gonna need to keep searching for solutions to, and if we can feel like we’ve tried everything that is reasonable, I think we’re gonna feel a little bit better about trying to manage the water resources for the district and for the water users within the district.”

passages: Executives have long dismissed the idea of a touchscreen Mac – but it is finally coming, and Apple is rumoured to have plans to fix its central problems

But Apple has more recently come to believe that the two could complement each other – with software, performance and versatility helping to keep them separate – and has also added Mac-style features to its recent updates to the iPad.
Apple is about to release a whole new product – one that it previously explicitly derided.
The company will launch its first touchscreen Mac during an event on Wednesday, according to numerous reports.
It will be a new version of the MacBook Pro , which will come with an upgraded display and a new lighter design in addition to its touch-sensitive screen, rumours suggest.

That criticism goes all the way back to 2010, when co-founder and former chief executive Steve Jobs described the idea as “ergonomically terrible”,.

But Apple has planned a host of changes to address those problems, new reports suggest. Chief among them is the idea that the touchscreen Mac will still be focused around the keyboard and trackpad as its primary interface, Bloomberg reported.

It will stress that the Mac is not becoming a touch-first computer and that the new model’s software will remain optimised for the usual experience, the report said. But it will also come with a new update to its Mac operating system, Golden Gate, aimed at making it easier to use with a finger.

The software will feature what Bloomberg calls a “dynamic interface”, which will be able to switch between the usual controls and those redesigned for touch, and remember which they have done more recently. The aim is to allow people to switch between the two input methods without thinking about it, Bloomberg reported.

The report suggested however that concerns about the ergonomics of using the device remain, and that some inside Apple had resisted the idea as a result. The company has been convinced by the idea that it could bring new customers to the Mac as well as help keep momentum around its line-up of computers – which had for a long time been losing ground in favour of its other products, but have come back in recent years because of working from home and its recent hardware advances.

There have also long been concerns that a touchscreen Mac could hurt sales of the iPad . But Apple has more recently come to believe that the two could complement each other – with software, performance and versatility helping to keep them separate – and has also added Mac-style features to its recent updates to the iPad.

The event on Wednesday follows a series of Apple launches in recent weeks, many of which introduced new kinds of products or innovative versions of its existing ones. The last two weeks alone have seen the introduction of the HomeView, a smart speaker with a display for inside people’s houses , as well as the release of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first folding device .

passages: If you had invested $1,000 in Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH), XRP (CRYPTO:XRP), or Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) five years ago, you bought in close to the peak of a major market rally.
Bitcoin closed October 2021 at $61,340 and hit a high of $68,770 in November 2021, shortly before the market began to decline.
As a result, investors bought all four cryptocurrencies near their highs.
Bitcoin emerged as the top performer, yielding a 36.6% gain over five years, while XRP followed closely with a 29.5% increase.
In contrast, Ethereum and Solana are still trading significantly below their prices from October 2021.
To break even, Ethereum would need to surpass $3,954, an increase of about 70%, and Solana would need to rise above $185, about 83% higher.
On the other hand, Ethereum fell 41.1%, reducing $1,000 to about $589, while Solana fell 45.1%, leaving about $549.
Even Ethereum and XRP investors faced significant losses after experiencing gains.
Unfortunately, both coins saw declines of 51.0% for XRP and 44.0% for Ethereum in the following year.
Over the past 90 days, all four coins have recovered some ground, with Bitcoin up 25.6% and Solana up 37.6%.
However, they are all still significantly down compared to a year ago.
Bitcoin may maintain its leading position as it has gained the most of these coins since 2021.
If Bitcoin stays above $79,107 (its low in October 2026), the initial $1,000 investment keeps showing a solid profit.
However, if it falls below $58,681, that gain could disappear entirely.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Its lowest monthly price during this period was $348 in October 2022, a 24% dip—much less severe than Bitcoin's or Solana's drops.
It then surged to its all-time high in October 2025, making that stake worth around $2,150.
It plummeted to a low of $8.12 in December 2022, cutting the initial investment down to about $44, a staggering 95.6% loss.
However, it rebounded to $295 in January 2025, bringing that stake back up to about $1,597.
Of the four cryptocurrencies, two gained value while two lost almost half their value.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) tracks large U.S. companies and closed at $459 in October 2021.

This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

If you had invested $1,000 in Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ), or Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) five years ago, you bought in close to the peak of a major market rally. Bitcoin closed October 2021 at $61,340 and hit a high of $68,770 in November 2021, shortly before the market began to decline. As a result, investors bought all four cryptocurrencies near their highs.
Over the past 90 days, all four coins have recovered some ground, with Bitcoin up 25.6% and Solana up 37.6%. However, they are all still significantly down compared to a year ago.
We examined a $1,000 investment in each coin made on October 27, 2021, and evaluated their worth recently. Of the four cryptocurrencies, two gained value while two lost almost half their value.
Bitcoin turned a $1,000 investment into about $1,366, a 36.6% increase over five years. XRP closely followed with a value of approximately $1,295 after a 29.5% gain.
On the other hand, Ethereum fell 41.1%, reducing $1,000 to about $589, while Solana fell 45.1%, leaving about $549.

If you had split your $1,000 investment equally among the four coins, with $250 in each, your total would be about $950 based on today’s price. The two gainers absorbed most of the losses from the two decliners, but the overall investment still lost money over five years.

Bitcoin’s journey was turbulent. At its June 2022 monthly low, Bitcoin fell to $17,698, dropping the initial $1,000 investment to about $302, a 69.8% decline. It then surged to its all-time high in October 2025, making that stake worth around $2,150.

Solana had an even more dramatic ride. It plummeted to a low of $8.12 in December 2022, cutting the initial investment down to about $44, a staggering 95.6% loss. However, it rebounded to $295 in January 2025, bringing that stake back up to about $1,597.

Even Ethereum and XRP investors faced significant losses after experiencing gains. In late October 2025, XRP was priced at $2.65, and Ethereum hit $4,159, both above their prices from October 2021. Unfortunately, both coins saw declines of 51.0% for XRP and 44.0% for Ethereum in the following year.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) tracks large U.S. companies and closed at $459 in October 2021. By October 23, 2026, it climbed to $760. With dividends reinvested, a $1,000 investment would have grown to about $1,770, for a total return of 77.0%—better than any of the cryptocurrencies mentioned.
The ETF also had a smoother ride. Its lowest monthly price during this period was $348 in October 2022, a 24% dip—much less severe than Bitcoin’s or Solana’s drops.

A dollar-cost averaging strategy—investing a fixed amount regularly regardless of price—would have helped as well. If you had invested $200 in Bitcoin at the end of each October from 2021 through 2025, you would have paid $61,340, $20,504, $34,650, $70,347, and $109,555 per coin.

Overall, those five investments would be worth about $1,880 based on recent prices, outperforming the one-time investment of $1,366 made in October 2021. The 2022 purchase played a crucial role because it bought Bitcoin near its market low.

Bitcoin emerged as the top performer, yielding a 36.6% gain over five years, while XRP followed closely with a 29.5% increase. In contrast, Ethereum and Solana are still trading significantly below their prices from October 2021. To break even, Ethereum would need to surpass $3,954, an increase of about 70%, and Solana would need to rise above $185, about 83% higher.

Meanwhile, an S&P 500 index fund outperformed all four cryptocurrencies, and the strategy of investing in Bitcoin over five years yielded the best result of the group. Bitcoin may maintain its leading position as it has gained the most of these coins since 2021. If Bitcoin stays above $79,107 (its low in October 2026), the initial $1,000 investment keeps showing a solid profit. However, if it falls below $58,681, that gain could disappear entirely.

facts.text: If you had invested $1,000 in Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH), XRP (CRYPTO:XRP), or Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) five years ago, you bought in close to the peak of a major market rally.
Bitcoin closed October 2021 at $61,340 and hit a high of $68,770 in November 2021, shortly before the market began to decline.
As a result, investors bought all four cryptocurrencies near their highs.
Bitcoin emerged as the top performer, yielding a 36.6% gain over five years, while XRP followed closely with a 29.5% increase.
In contrast, Ethereum and Solana are still trading significantly below their prices from October 2021.
To break even, Ethereum would need to surpass $3,954, an increase of about 70%, and Solana would need to rise above $185, about 83% higher.
On the other hand, Ethereum fell 41.1%, reducing $1,000 to about $589, while Solana fell 45.1%, leaving about $549.
Even Ethereum and XRP investors faced significant losses after experiencing gains.
Unfortunately, both coins saw declines of 51.0% for XRP and 44.0% for Ethereum in the following year.
Over the past 90 days, all four coins have recovered some ground, with Bitcoin up 25.6% and Solana up 37.6%.
However, they are all still significantly down compared to a year ago.
Bitcoin may maintain its leading position as it has gained the most of these coins since 2021.
If Bitcoin stays above $79,107 (its low in October 2026), the initial $1,000 investment keeps showing a solid profit.
However, if it falls below $58,681, that gain could disappear entirely.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Its lowest monthly price during this period was $348 in October 2022, a 24% dip—much less severe than Bitcoin's or Solana's drops.
It then surged to its all-time high in October 2025, making that stake worth around $2,150.
It plummeted to a low of $8.12 in December 2022, cutting the initial investment down to about $44, a staggering 95.6% loss.
However, it rebounded to $295 in January 2025, bringing that stake back up to about $1,597.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) tracks large U.S. companies and closed at $459 in October 2021.

Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles.
His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.
When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.

extraction.body: Early reviews and hands-on impressions of the new iPad mini came out today. Most publications agree that the iPad mini is a great update for fans of the smaller 7.9-inch tablet with almost identical tech specs to the new iPad Air . That includes the same A12 Bionic chip, 8-megapixel rear camera, 7-megapixel front camera, Touch ID , Lightning connector, 64GB and 256GB storage options, two speakers, headphone jack, Gigabit-class LTE, first-generation Apple Pencil compatibility, and up to 10 hours of battery life. The new ‌iPad mini‌'s only notable differences versus the new ‌iPad Air‌ are its smaller screen and lack of Smart Keyboard compatibility. As The Verge 's Nilay Patel notes, however, the ‌iPad mini‌ design is now very old: You're still looking at the exact same external design, which is now nearly seven years old. If you secretly replaced any previous iPad mini with the new one, there's a chance you might not even notice the difference. All the changes to this new mini are on the inside, and they're significant — which they should be, given the amount of time since it was last refreshed. And while the ‌iPad mini‌ finally supports the ‌Apple Pencil‌, it comes with all of the downsides of the first-generation version: …the iPad Pro came out late last year with a new second-gen pencil that magnetically clips onto the side of the iPad and charges wirelessly, but this new mini doesn’t have any of that. Instead, you’ve got Apple’s first-gen Pencil, which has never been a triumph of design or usability. You still pair and charge it by plugging it into the bottom of the iPad, which looks even more ridiculous on the mini, and the cap is still insanely easy to lose. As for the ‌iPad mini‌ sticking with the Lightning connector, Apple told Patel that it views USB-C as a "pro" feature — aka iPad Pro . Patel added that "the display is very nice" on the new ‌iPad mini‌ despite not having the ‌iPad Pro‌'s ProMotion variable refresh rate for smooth scrolling, but found that its same old 8-megapixel rear camera "takes at best medium-good photos." Most reviews conclude that if you want the smallest iPad possible, the new ‌iPad mini‌ is quite capable and at least somewhat reasonably priced at $399. And with little competition from Android tablets, the ‌iPad mini‌ is one of the only small tablets worthy of consideration in the first place. But the decision to get an iPad mini is simple: do you want a small, capable tablet? If you do, the mini is obviously worth $399, especially when you consider how long Apple has supported iPads for in the past. There’s just nothing else like it. Let’s just hope that next time we don’t have to wait four years for Apple to remember it exists again. I haven't fallen in love with the new Mini, just as I never felt the need to buy one before. But I could see why people would. It's less burdensome than a lot of other things we carry. It's not quite pocketable, but it's close. Again, I can't hold it in one hand, but some people can, I'm sure. The Mini feels personal in a way that other devices no longer do. Not because of its actual newness, but because it is still here, and slightly reinvented once again. It still looks like an iPad Mini–complete with home button and headphone jack. But after three loooooong years, Apple’s little tablet is finally getting the features it needs to qualify as a modern iPad. I'd actually argue it's perhaps the best small tablet out there right now. There's more than enough power here for most people, and if portability is your biggest concern, there's no denying the mini is more convenient to lug around. There simply isn't a tablet as powerful as the new iPad mini with the same or similar dimensions. You can get a 7-inch Kindle Fire for $50, but it's demonstrably inferior in every way from the construction, to the app selection, to the performance, to the storage, to display, and etc. An iPad Mini with a faster processor and Pencil support is filling a specific need not everyone will have. It's like a specifically sized screw, or a particular TV size. As Apple keeps splitting its iPad line into more variants, the Mini feels far less essential than ever, particularly as the iPhone screens creep to six inches or more. extraction.body: Early reviews and hands-on impressions of the new iPad mini came out today. Most publications agree that the iPad mini is a great update for fans of the smaller 7.9-inch tablet with almost identical tech specs to the new iPad Air . That includes the same A12 Bionic chip, 8-megapixel rear camera, 7-megapixel front camera, Touch ID , Lightning connector, 64GB and 256GB storage options, two speakers, headphone jack, Gigabit-class LTE, first-generation Apple Pencil compatibility, and up to 10 hours of battery life. The new ‌iPad mini‌'s only notable differences versus the new ‌iPad Air‌ are its smaller screen and lack of Smart Keyboard compatibility. As The Verge 's Nilay Patel notes, however, the ‌iPad mini‌ design is now very old: You're still looking at the exact same external design, which is now nearly seven years old. If you secretly replaced any previous iPad mini with the new one, there's a chance you might not even notice the difference. All the changes to this new mini are on the inside, and they're significant — which they should be, given the amount of time since it was last refreshed. And while the ‌iPad mini‌ finally supports the ‌Apple Pencil‌, it comes with all of the downsides of the first-generation version: …the iPad Pro came out late last year with a new second-gen pencil that magnetically clips onto the side of the iPad and charges wirelessly, but this new mini doesn’t have any of that. Instead, you’ve got Apple’s first-gen Pencil, which has never been a triumph of design or usability. You still pair and charge it by plugging it into the bottom of the iPad, which looks even more ridiculous on the mini, and the cap is still insanely easy to lose. As for the ‌iPad mini‌ sticking with the Lightning connector, Apple told Patel that it views USB-C as a "pro" feature — aka iPad Pro . Patel added that "the display is very nice" on the new ‌iPad mini‌ despite not having the ‌iPad Pro‌'s ProMotion variable refresh rate for smooth scrolling, but found that its same old 8-megapixel rear camera "takes at best medium-good photos." Most reviews conclude that if you want the smallest iPad possible, the new ‌iPad mini‌ is quite capable and at least somewhat reasonably priced at $399. And with little competition from Android tablets, the ‌iPad mini‌ is one of the only small tablets worthy of consideration in the first place. But the decision to get an iPad mini is simple: do you want a small, capable tablet? If you do, the mini is obviously worth $399, especially when you consider how long Apple has supported iPads for in the past. There’s just nothing else like it. Let’s just hope that next time we don’t have to wait four years for Apple to remember it exists again. I haven't fallen in love with the new Mini, just as I never felt the need to buy one before. But I could see why people would. It's less burdensome than a lot of other things we carry. It's not quite pocketable, but it's close. Again, I can't hold it in one hand, but some people can, I'm sure. The Mini feels personal in a way that other devices no longer do. Not because of its actual newness, but because it is still here, and slightly reinvented once again. It still looks like an iPad Mini–complete with home button and headphone jack. But after three loooooong years, Apple’s little tablet is finally getting the features it needs to qualify as a modern iPad. I'd actually argue it's perhaps the best small tablet out there right now. There's more than enough power here for most people, and if portability is your biggest concern, there's no denying the mini is more convenient to lug around. There simply isn't a tablet as powerful as the new iPad mini with the same or similar dimensions. You can get a 7-inch Kindle Fire for $50, but it's demonstrably inferior in every way from the construction, to the app selection, to the performance, to the storage, to display, and etc. An iPad Mini with a faster processor and Pencil support is filling a specific need not everyone will have. It's like a specifically sized screw, or a particular TV size. As Apple keeps splitting its iPad line into more variants, the Mini feels far less essential than ever, particularly as the iPhone screens creep to six inches or more. sources.title: Apple acknowledges iPhone Duo display ‘issue’ after reports of cracked screens
passages: Following reports of iPhone Duos with cracked and broken inside screens, often showing a bright line running from the center to the right side, Apple says in a statement to Bloomberg and 9to5Mac that it’s aware of “an issue impacting the inner display” on a “small number of iPhone Duo units.” If your iPhone Duo is affected, Apple says to contact AppleCare for a replacement.
Shortly after launch, iPhone Duo users started reporting similar issues where the hinge would tighten, and opening the device caused a crack and the distinctive bright lines on the display.

passages: Apple on Monday announced a new iPad mini with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display.
The tablet features a thinner and lighter design than its predecessor and is powered by an A20 Pro chip.
The tech giant revealed the new device just days before its “Pro and Tell” event that’s scheduled to take place on Wednesday.
Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, the iPad mini has up to 4.5-times faster AI performance than the previous generation, according to Apple.
It also features an “Acoustic Display” that Apple says enhances the audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content.
Specially designed woofers integrated into the display deliver deeper bass and higher volume for richer sound, per the company.
The Super Retina XDR display uses OLED technology for pixel-level lighting control, delivering deeper blacks, richer contrast, and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vibrant colors.

extraction.body: Apple on Monday announced a new iPad mini with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display. The tablet features a thinner and lighter design than its predecessor and is powered by an A20 Pro chip. The new iPad mini starts at $699 for the Wi-Fi model and $849 for the Wi-Fi and cellular model. The tech giant revealed the new device just days before its “Pro and Tell” event that’s scheduled to take place on Wednesday. The new iPad mini is 5.4 mm in thickness, and available in two colors. The device delivers peak brightness of up to 1,200 nits, more than twice that of the previous-generation device, along with full screen brightness of 600 nits for SDR and HDR content and a 2 million:1 contrast ratio. Apple says the iPad mini is ideal for dim-light environments. The iPad mini also comes with a new nano-texture display option that reduces glare in bright environments, a feature already available on the iPad Pro. The updated tablet now also features a 12-megapixel center stage front camera, faster wireless and cellular connectivity, and fast-charge support. The Super Retina XDR display uses OLED technology for pixel-level lighting control, delivering deeper blacks, richer contrast, and support for the P3 wide color gamut for more vibrant colors. It also features an “Acoustic Display” that Apple says enhances the audio experience when gaming, watching videos, or editing content. Specially designed woofers integrated into the display deliver deeper bass and higher volume for richer sound, per the company. The new iPad mini launches with the next generation of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, which can draw on a user’s personal context to help them find what they need, answer questions, and understand what’s on their screen. Powered by a 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, the iPad mini has up to 4.5-times faster AI performance than the previous generation, according to Apple. The A20 Pro also features a 6-core CPU, delivering up to 60% faster multithreaded performance for everyday tasks such as photo editing and multitasking across apps. The device can be preordered on October 28, with availability beginning November 6. Aisha is a consumer news reporter at TechCrunch. passages: In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20x as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing.
The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.
Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working.
More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year.
Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.

Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”
Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams.

An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward-deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.
The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them.
The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.
Uber began by selling rides but has expanded into food delivery and freight.
With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave.

“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday , reads.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

“An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps.

The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers and then Cowork to their broader workforce.

Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20x as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API.

Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward-deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude.

Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.”

Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.”

The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in.

“Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.
